title: ETGS: Explicit Thermodynamics Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Thermal Reconstruction
one_liner: Embed heat-transfer physics directly into 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct scenes that change over time as temperature evolves.
lead: Imagine photographing a cup of tea cooling down from multiple angles over seconds, mixing thermal images with regular photos. The paper solves a hard problem: how do you reconstruct a 3D scene when its shape does not change but its temperature does, moment by moment? Previous methods ignore the physics of heat flow; this paper bakes it in, so the model learns to predict temperature change more accurately because it is constrained to follow the same exponential decay law that governs real heat loss.

problem.h2: Reconstructing a scene that only changes its temperature
paras: The world contains thermal events: cooling, heating, heat transfer between objects. A camera that sees both regular light (RGB) and infrared heat (IR) captures these changes. The naive approach: treat each photo as a separate snapshot and stitch them all together. That breaks because it does not understand that temperature evolves by a smooth physical law — it treats yesterday's temperature and tomorrow's as unrelated guesses, wasting the signal that heat moves predictably.

Existing 3D reconstruction methods assume the shape stays frozen and only the appearance (color, lighting) shifts. But thermal reconstruction is different: the shape is fixed, and temperature is the appearance that changes. The naive learner has no way to say 'temperature tomorrow will be lower because of heat loss' — it just memorizes each snapshot independently.

callout.html: The paper gives each 3D point a thermal model — a formula describing how its temperature changes over time — instead of just guessing each temperature independently.

panels.title: 1. The problem: many cameras, many moments
panels.caption: RGB and thermal cameras see the same 3D scene at different times.

panels.title: 2. Naive approach fails: treat each snapshot alone
panels.caption: Each moment's temperature is guessed independently with no connection to physics.

panels.title: 3. The paper's move: embed a heat-transfer model
panels.caption: Each 3D point carries a thermal formula that predicts how hot it is now.

panels.title: 4. Physics constrains the learning
panels.caption: The model only adjusts the thermal formulas; shape and physics stay locked.

panels.title: 5. Payoff: rapid temperature changes are captured accurately
panels.caption: Cooling, heating, and heat transfer between objects emerge from the learned numbers.

steps.text: Each point in the scene gets two things: a color (like RGB Gaussian Splatting) and a thermal number that describes how it cools.

steps.b: Equip each point with a heat-transfer formula
steps.text: Instead of storing a fixed temperature, store the rate at which it cools (or heats). This is a simple equation like initial_temp minus cooling_rate times elapsed_time.

steps.b: Render both RGB and thermal images
steps.text: At any timestamp, evaluate the thermal formula for each point. Blend all visible points to create a thermal image, just like blending colors in normal Gaussian Splatting.
Compare rendered thermal images to real IR photos. Use backpropagation (gradient descent) to adjust the cooling rates and initial temperatures until the formulas predict the data accurately.

steps.b: Render at any time, including between observations
steps.text: Because the formula is analytical (closed-form), you can ask for the temperature at any moment without numerical solving — 10ms, 500ms, or any time you want.

object.h2: The thing the paper changes: thermal formulas baked into the model
paras: Each 3D point in the reconstruction now carries not just a color but a thermal evolution equation. Instead of training the model to guess independent temperatures for each moment, the paper trains it to learn the coefficients of a heat-transfer formula. The object is the thermal formula per point — specifically, the starting temperature and cooling rate (the two numbers that define the formula).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: how fast does heat leave each point?
hidden.name: Cooling rate (or thermal time-constant)
paras: The paper measures a quantity usually invisible in thermal images: the rate at which each 3D point loses (or gains) heat over time. In the real world, this depends on the material, the surface area, and the surrounding environment. The paper does not model all that; instead, it lets the model learn one number per point: the effective cooling rate, a hidden quantity that summarizes 'how fast does this point approach ambient temperature?'

The paper infers this rate by fitting the heat-transfer formula to the observed temperatures across all the captured moments. If a region cools slowly, the learned rate is low; if it cools fast, the learned rate is high. This learned rate then becomes the mechanism for rendering accurate thermal images at any time, including moments between observations.

heat.caption: Darker means faster cooling rate. High rates (hot cells) cool quickly; low rates (light cells) hold heat longer.

reads.html: Each point cools at its own speed, described by one number that the model learns from the data.
The thermal value per Gaussian encodes the time-constant of exponential heat loss, estimated via the closed-form solution of the heat-transfer ODE during training.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: physics as a learning constraint
paras: The trick is using an analytical solution to the heat-transfer equation. Instead of numerically solving a differential equation at render time (which is slow and noisy), the paper uses a closed-form formula: temperature at time t equals initial_temperature minus an exponential decay. This formula has only two unknowns per point: the starting temperature and the cooling rate. Training then becomes: adjust these two numbers until the formula predicts all the observed temperatures.

Why does this beat naive memorization? Because the formula forces the model to learn a smooth, physically plausible thermal trajectory. A Gaussian point cannot 'jump' in temperature or cool backwards; it must follow the exponential law. This constraint is a feature: it is a strong inductive bias that says 'temperature evolves like heat in the real world.' The model learns the rate faster and with less data because it is not wasting its leeway (degrees of freedom, just two numbers per point) on thermal wobble that violates physics.

Irregular or out-of-order observations (camera 1 sees 10ms, camera 2 sees 20ms, then camera 1 again at 25ms) become easy to handle. The formula evaluates at any timestamp, so the learning algorithm simply pulls each observation's expected temperature from the formula and compares. No need to interpolate or reorder the data.

stages.s: RGB and thermal images at irregular times
Extract 3D shape (where the Gaussians are and what color they are)
Assign each point an initial temperature and cooling rate
For each observation time, evaluate the heat-transfer formula
Render thermal image by blending all visible points
Predicted thermal image; backprop adjusts the thermal numbers

math.words: Temperature at time t equals the starting temperature minus the difference (starting minus ambient) times an exponential decay factor.
symbols: temperature at time t (what we want to predict)
initial temperature at time zero (learned per point)
elapsed time since the start of the sequence
thermal time-constant (how fast cooling happens, learned per point)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say room temperature is 20 degrees. A hot object starts at 100 degrees (T_0 = 100). Its time-constant is tau = 2 seconds.
At t=0: T(0) = 20 + (100 - 20) * exp(0) = 20 + 80 * 1 = 100 degrees. Correct — it starts hot.
At t=2: T(2) = 20 + 80 * exp(-2/2) = 20 + 80 * exp(-1) = 20 + 80 * 0.368 = 20 + 29.4 = 49.4 degrees. Half the excess heat is gone.
At t=6: T(6) = 20 + 80 * exp(-6/2) = 20 + 80 * exp(-3) = 20 + 80 * 0.050 = 20 + 4 = 24 degrees. Nearly room temperature.
The same point's temperature drops fast at first (100 to 49 in 2 seconds) and slows as it approaches room temp. This exponential shape is what the paper lets the model learn.

math.note: The model learns the starting temperature and cooling rate for each point so that the formula predicts all observed thermal images. No numerical solving needed at render time — just plug in the elapsed time and compute.

charts.title: Static baseline (ignores thermal dynamics)
charts.note: A static 3DGS model learns one fixed temperature per point. It tries to average across all times, so it is wrong for early, middle, and late frames. It cannot capture rapid dynamics.

charts.title: This paper (ETGS with learned dynamics)
charts.note: By learning the cooling rate per point, the model predicts temperature accurately across the entire sequence. It handles rapid thermal changes because it is constrained by physics.

items.b: Assumption of exponential decay breaks if an external heat source arrives.
items.html: If a heater turns on halfway through the sequence, the temperature will start rising instead of falling. The exponential model cannot capture this change of regime. The paper assumes the thermal process stays stationary (no new heat sources or sinks entering the scene).

items.b: The model is sensitive to the assumed ambient temperature.
items.html: If you set the room temperature wrong, the learned cooling rates will be garbage. The paper does not discuss how to estimate this in practice — it must be supplied or calibrated.

items.b: Irregular or very sparse observations can lead to poor calibration.
items.html: If thermal images come in large time gaps, the exponential formula may fit many different (starting temperature, cooling rate) pairs equally well. The model might converge to a wrong solution. Dense temporal sampling helps because tightly-spaced observations lock down the cooling rate unambiguously.

When observations are dense and fairly regular, the ambient temperature is known, and the thermal process is genuinely passive cooling or heating (no external interventions), the method works well. The learned rates become interpretable and accurate.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic scene: a 3D object (like a teapot) with an initial temperature. Simulate the physics — each point cools exponentially toward room temperature, with different rates for different materials. Generate RGB-IR image pairs at 10 millisecond intervals for 5 seconds. Train ETGS on these pairs. At test time, render the scene at timestamps it has never seen (e.g., 2.3ms, 3.7ms) and measure how close the rendered thermal image is to the ground-truth simulated image.
demo.metric_eq: Thermal MAE = mean absolute error of predicted vs. ground-truth temperature, summed over all pixels and test times
demo.closing: The key observation: ETGS's thermal prediction at unseen times is accurate (error close to the simulated noise level), whereas a naive static model or a frame-independent baseline will be visibly wrong — ghosting, blurring, or temperature inversions at new times.
